tagline: One of Germany's last never-destroyed Staufer castles, home to a real birds-of-prey centre — but the bookable stay is a self-catering house for up to 19, a separate building 50 metres from the castle itself
highlights: One of the last never-destroyed, continuously inhabited Staufer-era castles in Germany — founded around 1180, held by the Gemmingen-Guttenberg family since the mid-15th century, nearly 800 years of unbroken history

Not to be confused with other German castles sharing the Guttenberg name — there are separate, unrelated Burg Guttenberg sites in Bavaria (Oberfranken and near Würzburg) and the Palatinate; this one is specifically in Neckarmühlbach, Baden-Württemberg, on the Neckar

Home to the Deutsche Greifenwarte (German birds of prey centre), established 1971, with regular live flight demonstrations of birds of prey and owls — one of the strongest genuine day-visitor draws of any castle in this project

The bookable accommodation itself is a separate self-catering vacation house ("Greifenreich"), about 50 metres from the castle, sleeping up to 19 people across 5 rooms — booked as a whole property, not by individual room
description:
Burg Guttenberg was founded around 1180 above Neckarmühlbach in Baden-Württemberg, with its first documented mention dating to 1296. What sets it apart from nearly every other castle in this collection is continuity: it is one of the last Staufer-era castles in Germany never to have been destroyed, and it has been continuously inhabited for close to 800 years, held since the mid-15th century by the Gemmingen-Guttenberg line of the Freiherren von Gemmingen family. Travelers researching this castle online should note that several other, unrelated sites in Germany also carry the Guttenberg name — including ruined and rebuilt castles in Bavaria and the Palatinate — none connected to this Neckar valley property.

In the 20th century, Gustav von Gemmingen-Guttenberg opened the castle to tourism in 1923, established a castle museum in 1949 and a castle tavern in 1950, and in 1971 brought in the Deutsche Greifenwarte, a birds-of-prey centre that remains one of the castle's biggest draws today, with regular live flight demonstrations of eagles, falcons, and owls. The specific accommodation bookable through this listing, however, is not inside the castle at all: it's a self-catering vacation house called "Greifenreich," roughly 50 metres from Burg Guttenberg, sleeping up to 19 people across five bedrooms and 300 square metres spread over three floors — booked and priced as a complete property rather than by individual room, and entirely separate from access to the castle's museum, tavern, or birds-of-prey shows.

The castle's unbroken 800-year continuity as an inhabited, never-destroyed structure makes it a genuine rarity within German castle history, where war, fire and deliberate demolition have left the great majority of medieval fortifications as ruins, later reconstructions, or buildings substantially rebuilt after significant damage. Guttenberg's survival intact through the Thirty Years' War, the Napoleonic period and two World Wars places it in a distinct category from almost every other property covered in this collection.

The Deutsche Greifenwarte's 1971 founding reflects a broader mid-20th-century trend of German castles developing dedicated wildlife or historical attractions to sustain public interest and visitor revenue beyond simple architectural tourism, and the birds-of-prey centre's regular flight demonstrations have become one of the most consistently recommended family day trips in this part of Baden-Württemberg, independent of Guttenberg's own accommodation options.

The Gemmingen family's continuous ownership since the 15th century connects Guttenberg to the same broader Franconian and Swabian noble network responsible for several other castles in this collection, including Hornberg Castle further down the Neckar, also long held by a branch of the Gemmingen family — a genuine historical link between two properties in this directory rather than a coincidental naming overlap.

The Greifenreich vacation house's whole-property booking model, sleeping up to 19 guests across five bedrooms, positions it closer to a large group or multi-family holiday rental than to any other accommodation type covered elsewhere in this collection, including Stahleck's per-person hostel pricing — Greifenreich is priced and booked as a single unit regardless of how many of its beds are actually filled.

Neckarmühlbach's position within the Neckar-Odenwald district places Guttenberg within a stretch of the Neckar valley already covered by Hornberg Castle in this collection, giving visitors interested in the region's castle-dense stretch of river a natural opportunity to combine both properties, along with the historic towns of Bad Wimpfen and Heidelberg further along the same valley.
history: Burg Guttenberg was founded around 1180 above Neckarmühlbach in Baden-Württemberg and is one of the last Staufer-era castles in Germany never to have been destroyed, continuously inhabited for close to 800 years and held since the mid-15th century by the Gemmingen-Guttenberg family. The castle opened to tourism in 1923, added a museum in 1949 and the Deutsche Greifenwarte birds-of-prey centre in 1971. The bookable accommodation, a separate self-catering vacation house called "Greifenreich" roughly 50 metres from the castle, sleeps up to 19 people and is booked as a whole property rather than by individual room.

faqs.question: Does booking the vacation house at Guttenberg include access to the castle?
faqs.answer: No. Burg Guttenberg itself — including the Deutsche Greifenwarte birds-of-prey centre, the castle museum, and the tavern — requires separate, on-site tickets and is not included with the Greifenreich vacation-house booking.

faqs.question: Is this a per-room hotel booking?
faqs.answer: No. The "Greifenreich" listing is a whole self-catering vacation house, sleeping up to 19 people across 5 bedrooms, booked and priced as a complete property (from roughly €400/night Monday–Friday, from €800/night Friday–Sunday) rather than by individual room or per person.

faqs.question: Is this the same Guttenberg as other German castles with that name?
faqs.answer: No. There are several unrelated German castles named Guttenberg, including sites in Bavaria (Oberfranken and near Würzburg) and the Palatinate. This Burg Guttenberg is specifically in Neckarmühlbach, Baden-Württemberg, on the Neckar river.

hotel.non_guest_access_note: Burg Guttenberg itself (not the vacation house) houses the Deutsche Greifenwarte — a real, ticketed birds-of-prey centre with live flight demonstrations (adults €15, children €11) — plus a separately ticketed castle museum (adults €7, children €5) and tavern, none included with the vacation-house booking.
hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** In Neckarmühlbach, part of Haßmersheim, Neckar-Odenwald district, Baden-Württemberg; about 45 minutes from Heidelberg and an hour from Stuttgart by car.

**Rooms & rates:** This is a whole-property self-catering house ("Greifenreich"), not a per-room hotel booking — sleeps up to 19 across 5 bedrooms. From €400/night Monday–Friday; from €800/night Friday–Sunday, varying by season (verify against live rate).

**On-site:** The vacation house itself is self-catering with no restaurant; Burg Guttenberg, about 50 metres away, has its own tavern, castle museum, and the Deutsche Greifenwarte birds-of-prey centre — all separately ticketed.

**Good to know:** This booking is for a self-catering vacation house near the castle, not a room inside Burg Guttenberg itself, and it is priced and booked per property (for a group), not per room or per person. The castle's museum and birds-of-prey flight shows require separate, on-site tickets and are not included.

**Combine with:** The Bad Wimpfen and Heidelberg castle circuit along the Neckar valley, both within easy driving distance.
